idiom_name: readonly state types + structuredClone snapshots with a typed history stack
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds compile-time guarantees rather than a runtime copy: model the originator's state as a readonly interface or Readonly<T> (readonly is shallow and erased at runtime) and the memento as that same type, so a `const history: State[]` cannot be written through. Snapshots themselves come from structuredClone, which is typed as returning the input type - a claim that holds for plain data and not for class instances, whose prototype chain the structured clone algorithm does not walk, so rehydration belongs to the originator. Discriminated-union actions plus a typed reducer give type-safe undo/redo: the history stores states, the actions describe transitions, and the compiler checks that every transition is handled. Persistence follows the JavaScript variant (JSON or structured-clone payloads) with a DTO type that is validated on load.
pitfalls: readonly is enforced at compile time only and is shallow: a nested object typed as readonly can still be mutated through an alias, and runtime code sees no protection at all.

structuredClone is typed as returning the input type even when it returns plain data (no prototype, no private fields), so a declared class-typed snapshot can be a lie - model snapshots as data interfaces, not class instances.

Excess-property and spread typing make it easy to widen a state accidentally (spreading an action into the state adds fields the type does not mention); apply actions through an explicit switch instead of an untyped spread.
A typed history array still grows without bound at runtime; the type system will not warn about memory.
